passage: I share a flat with Vasudha, so I was there when she wrote to the alumnus. She had read his profile for a whole evening, then wrote only four lines. First: who she is, a third-year student. Second: a sentence about his article on reading logs, which she said helped her project. Third: "Would you be open to a call of fifteen minutes, or, if easier, one question by message?" Fourth: thanks. She read it aloud to me and cut two lines that sounded too eager. I do not know if she was nervous; she kept tapping her pen. She sent it at nine. By noon the next day he had answered with a time on Saturday. — Siddharth

Sunday. Jatin's draft to Akash, a product designer at a studio in Bengaluru, runs to three paragraphs. His friend reads it and says, 'He'll stop at line two.' Jatin cuts it to four lines: 'I'm Jatin, a second-year design student in Indore. Your case study on the bus-ticket app made me redraw my own project's menus. Could I ask you one question, over a short fifteen-minute call, or by message if easier? Completely fine if you're busy.'
Wednesday. No reply. Jatin checks twice, then makes himself close the chat and work on his assignment.
Friday. A notification: 'Happy to. Send the question here, I'll answer tonight.' Jatin sends one question about testing menus with real users. At 10 p.m. Akash replies with three tips and a rough sketch.

qa.q: How does Jatin describe himself in the message?
qa.a: As a second-year design student in Indore.

qa.q: How was Jatin feeling on Wednesday, and what did he do?
qa.a: He was probably anxious and impatient, checking twice, but he made himself close the chat and get on with his assignment.

qa.q: What else could keep Jatin's messages this easy to answer?
qa.a: Keep to one clear ask with a polite way to say no, and send the actual question at once when the person prefers messages.

qa.q: How might the short message look to Akash?
qa.a: For Akash it is quick to read and easy to agree to, since it names his own case study and asks for very little.

passage:
Sunaina, you've been writing that message for an hour. Stop. Let me, Salma, tell you what my first mentor taught me when I was trying to reach an architect I admired.
My first letter, and it was a real paper letter then, ran to two pages. My life story, my marks, my dreams. No reply. My mentor, Kaveri madam, read my copy and laughed kindly. 'Four lines,' she said. 'Who you are. One thing of hers you genuinely liked, and why. One small request, fifteen minutes or one question. And a door to say no.'
So I wrote: I am a student in Lucknow; your library building made me want to design public spaces; could I ask you one question about its courtyard; I understand if you have no time. She wrote back in ten days and gave me forty minutes.
So. Four lines. Show me.

qa.q: How long was Salma's first letter?
How might Salma have felt when the two-page letter got no reply?
qa.a: Salma was probably disappointed and a little embarrassed, which made showing it to Kaveri madam feel like a risk.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed the result?
qa.a: Following Kaveri madam's four-line advice, with one small request and a way to say no, turned silence into a forty-minute meeting.

qa.q: How might the architect have seen the four-line letter?
qa.a: It was easy to say yes to, because it named her library building and asked for just one question.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a four-line letter to a stranger with who the writer was, a specific compliment and a small request that was easy to refuse.
